narrative:
Your law school application was denied because our predictive model, which assesses the likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first try, estimated a 51% chance that you would fail it. This prediction is based on patterns from thousands of past students' academic records, family backgrounds, and other factors, excluding gender and race. For you, a female white student from a lower-middle income family planning to attend part-time with an LSAT score of 34 and a strong undergraduate GPA of 3.70, the model highlighted three key factors that shaped this close-call decision.

The most influential factor pushing toward a failure prediction was your Year 3 decile ranking of 1st, which is much lower than the 5.91 average among students who passed the bar—suggesting your later academic performance in school raised concerns about sustaining the rigor needed for bar success. Counterbalancing this, your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 stood out positively, well above the 3.24 average for bar passers, showing the model recognized your strong foundation from undergrad as a clear strength pulling toward passing. Your LSAT score of 34 also helped in the same way, though it fell short of the 37.27 average for successful students, still contributing favorably compared to what might have dragged the prediction down further.

These elements outweighed other details like your family income bracket, which is less common among bar passers (only 9.4% in lower-middle versus 45.1% upper-middle), and your part-time status, rare among passers at just 6.8%. Overall, your low Year 3 decile was the dominant concern, tipping the scales despite your impressive undergrad record and decent LSAT. To improve your chances next time, focus on boosting your later-year grades to climb those decile rankings, perhaps by seeking tutoring or lighter course loads early on. Retaking the LSAT for a score closer to 37 or higher could also strengthen your profile significantly. Consider full-time enrollment if feasible, as it aligns better with bar success patterns, and gather letters highlighting your undergrad strengths. Reapplying after addressing these could flip the prediction in your favor.
